title: How does a neural network learn?
question: Nobody writes the rules for the AI you use every day. So how does it learn?
audience: Curious teens and adults anywhere who use AI every day (chatbots, photo filters, recommendations) but have never seen inside one. They have heard that 'AI is trained', but not what actually changes when it learns.
promise: A neural network learns by guessing, measuring how wrong the guess is (the error), and nudging every weight a little in the direction that makes the error smaller, over and over; nobody writes its rules.

loop.line: Again and again. That's how / the AI you use learned what it knows.
loop.picture: The last shot's loop arrow becomes the phone outline of s01 and the network redraws inside it, pulses in their frame-0 places: the same picture as frame 0.

look.mood: The Neon Line template: near-black #07070c with a faint perspective grid fading into the distance; single continuous glowing lines 3 to 4 px with round caps, outlines only, strong bloom, a little chromatic aberration at the edges, fine grain. Two neon colours with fixed meanings for the whole film: cyan #00f5d4 is the network (its nodes, its lines, the signal going down and the guess); magenta #f15bb5 is the error and everything it sends back (the gap, the backward pulses, the nudge arrows). White #e9fffb for type and the examples' drawings. Line width means weight. Captions: 'pop', two or three glowing white words at a time, the key word in magenta, the second neon colour, as the template's Captions line and its concept still have it (film.css sets .caption .key to #f15bb5 over the look's cyan); in the picture magenta only ever means the error. On the board cyan and magenta are drawn in darker teal and pink so they read on paper.

music.track: Composed for this film (ElevenLabs Music, music/bed.mp3)
music.note: A synth bed composed for the film at 96 BPM, as the template's Sound line asks: a pulsing sub bass on every beat, a warm analogue pad, a soft arpeggio that climbs when the guess runs down the network and falls when the error runs back; it thins under the error (s09 to s12), doubles its bass for the repetition (s14), opens wide for the scale shot (s18) and runs on past the last frame into the opening for the loop. Every shot is a whole number of beats, so every cut lands on the beat. Effects: soft zaps when pulses fire, a hum under the glowing network, a power-up buzz for the type, a low buzz for the error, a reversed zap for the backward pass, a synth swell for each nudge, blips for each example and result.

facts.claim: The AI people use is machine learning: instead of programmers writing the rules for the task, a model is trained on data until it has learned the relationship itself. Simplification: engineers still write the training program, choose the data and check the result; what nobody writes is the rules for the task ('if it meows → cat').
facts.source: Google, Machine Learning: Introduction to ML, 'What is ML?' (developers.google.com/machine-learning/intro-to-ml/what-is-ml): 'ML is the process of training a piece of software, called a model, to make useful predictions or generate content ... from data', contrasted there with the traditional approach of writing the model by hand.

facts.claim: A neural network is nodes (neurons) in layers, joined by connections; each neuron takes the sum of its inputs times a weight per connection, plus a bias, and passes it through an activation function. A weight is how strongly a connection passes its input on. In s05 the two lines are two of the toy network's starting weights, 0.92 and 0.28 (their sizes; the sign is not shown).
facts.source: Google Machine Learning Crash Course, 'Neural networks: Nodes and hidden layers' (developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/neural-networks/nodes-hidden-layers): 'take the sum of the product of each of its inputs ... and a unique weight parameter, plus the bias'.

facts.claim: The film's network is a real toy, trained in storyboard.build.py: three yes/no inputs (meow?, bark?, four legs?: 1 = yes, 0 = no), three hidden neurons and one output, sigmoid activations, 12 weights (the lines drawn) plus 4 biases (not drawn). Three examples: cat (1, 0, 1) → 1, dog (0, 1, 1) → 0, fish (0, 0, 0) → 0. Starting weights and biases random between −1 and 1 (seeded, seed 8), as training usually starts. Line widths are drawn from the sizes of the weights. Simplification: real image networks read millions of pixel values, not three yes/no answers; this one is small enough to watch.
facts.source: Computed (storyboard.build.py). Method: Google ML Crash Course, 'Linear regression: Gradient descent' ('The model begins training with randomized weights and biases near zero'); Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986), 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors', Nature 323, 533–536.

facts.claim: The first guess for the cat is 0.269 → shown as 0.27; the right answer is 1, so the gap (the error) is 1 − 0.27 = 0.73. The film calls the gap 'error'; training makes the squared gap small (squared error), which is the same aim. 'Loss is a numerical value indicating the difference between a model's predictions and the actual values.'
facts.source: Computed (storyboard.build.py); Google ML Crash Course, 'Linear regression: Loss' (developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/linear-regression/loss).

facts.claim: Learning is gradient descent: work out, for every weight, which way to move it to make the error smaller, move it a small amount that way, and repeat. Backpropagation is how a network works out that direction for every weight: the error is sent backwards from the output through the connections. 'The procedure repeatedly adjusts the weights of the connections in the network so as to minimize a measure of the difference between the actual output vector of the net and the desired output vector.'
facts.source: Google ML Crash Course, 'Linear regression: Gradient descent' (steps: calculate the loss, determine the direction that reduces it, move the weights and bias a small amount, repeat) and 'Neural networks: Training using backpropagation' ('Backpropagation is the most common training algorithm for neural networks'); Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986), Nature 323, 533–536, abstract.

facts.claim: One nudge (one gradient step on the cat, step size 2.0): the weight from the middle hidden neuron to the output goes 0.661 → 0.791 (shown 0.66 → 0.79), every other weight touched by the error moves too, and the guess for the same cat goes 0.27 → 0.40: the error 0.73 → 0.60. The step size (learning rate) is set large in this toy so one step is visible; real training takes much smaller steps.
facts.source: Computed (storyboard.build.py); learning rate: Google ML Crash Course, 'Linear regression: Hyperparameters' ('The learning rate determines the magnitude of the changes to make to the weights and bias during each step').

facts.claim: Repeated over the three examples for 1,000 rounds (one nudge per example per round), the network's answers become cat 0.983, dog 0.009, fish 0.015 (shown 0.98, 0.01, 0.01). The mean squared error over the three falls from 0.227 to 0.00019; the chart in s15 shows its first 60 rounds, after which it lies flat (it is below 0.01 by round 50). A loss curve that falls and flattens is what training looks like. As built, the chart in s15 plots the cat's own error (1 − its guess, the gap the meter shows): 0.73 at the start, 0.60 after the one nudge, 0.64 after round 1, 0.10 at round 60, and 0.02 after round 1,000 (written at the right end of the chart), so its numbers continue the meter's; the mean squared error above is the measure training itself makes small.
facts.source: Computed (storyboard.build.py); Google ML Crash Course, 'Linear regression: Gradient descent' (loss curves; 'A model is considered to have converged when further iterations do not significantly reduce the loss').

facts.claim: Nobody set which input matters. At the start the lines from 'bark?' were the strongest (sum of the three weights' sizes: meow 1.95, bark 2.34, four legs 1.54); after training the lines from 'meow?' are (meow 7.10, bark 4.53, four legs 3.47). In the three examples, meowing is what tells a cat apart. This is the toy's result; in big networks what each weight 'means' is usually not readable like this.
facts.source: Computed (storyboard.build.py); Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986): as a result of the weight adjustments, hidden units 'come to represent important features of the task domain'.

facts.claim: Big models learn the same way, with far more weights: GPT-3 (2020) has 175 billion parameters (on screen '175,000,000,000' and '175 billion weights'), trained with Adam (a form of gradient descent) on 300 billion tokens; its 'error' is how wrong its guess of the next word is. Against the toy's 12 weights the drawing cannot be to scale and says so; the zoom-out passes a field of a million weights on the way, a scale mark between the two and not any particular model. Simplifications: the film calls parameters 'weights' (they also include biases and embeddings), and Adam adjusts each step's size, but each step still moves the weights to reduce the error.
facts.source: Brown et al. (2020), 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners', arXiv:2005.14165: 'we train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters'; §2.3 and Appendix B: 'All models were trained for a total of 300 billion tokens'; 'To train all versions of GPT-3, we use Adam'.

acts.title: The question
acts.goal: The AI you use learned; nobody wrote its rules. Then how?

acts.title: Weights
acts.goal: Inside: nodes and connections; each connection has a weight.

acts.title: A guess
acts.goal: A toy network: an example goes in, a guess comes out.

acts.title: The error
acts.goal: The guess against the answer: the gap is the error.

acts.title: Nudge
acts.goal: The error goes back; every weight is nudged a little; the next guess is closer.

acts.title: Repeat
acts.goal: Repeated a thousand times: the error falls, the answers come right, the weights find what matters; big models do the same.

acts.title: The answer
acts.goal: Guess, measure, nudge, repeat; then the bridge into the first line.

shots.caption: The AI you use *learned* what it knows.

shots.caption: Here's a tiny one. Its job: is it a *cat*?
shots.teaches: A tiny network to watch learn: three yes/no questions in, one guess out: is it a cat?
shots.screen: The toy network, stacked top to bottom: three input nodes at y 500 labelled above them 'meow?', 'bark?', 'four legs?'; three hidden nodes at y 790; one output node at y 1070 labelled 'cat?' at its right. Twelve cyan lines, each as wide as its starting weight (random, between 0 and 1).
shots.motion: Pull back from the two lines; the nodes pop on with a flicker, top row first; the twelve lines draw on fast; the labels write on.
shots.transition: Continuous: an example drops in from the top.
shots.sound: A rising run of three blips for the three rows.
shots.check: Twelve lines, three plus three plus one nodes; widths differ, as the weights do.

frames.note: Pull back: the nodes pop on, row by row.
The twelve lines draw on, each as wide as its weight.
Labelled: three questions in, 'cat?' out.

shots.caption: First example: a *cat*.
shots.teaches: The first example goes in: a cat: it meows (1), doesn't bark (0), has four legs (1).
shots.screen: A cat drawn in one white outline line drops in at the top (y 210 to 340); the three inputs show their answers inside the nodes: '1', '0', '1'; the '0' node stays dim.
shots.motion: The cat outline draws on in one stroke; three short white lines flick from it to the inputs; each input node flickers on with its number (the '0' one stays dark).
shots.carries: The network with the cat's answers in it.
shots.transition: Continuous: the signal leaves the inputs.
shots.sound: A soft chirp as the cat draws; three blips, the middle one muted.
shots.check: The inputs read 1, 0, 1, matching meow, bark, four legs for a cat.

frames.note: The cat outline draws on at the top.
The answers in the inputs: 1, 0, 1.

shots.caption: The signal flows through to a *guess*.
shots.teaches: The signal flows through every weight and comes out as a guess.
shots.screen: (As built: the camera rides the signal down; as it reaches the hidden row each node shows its value, 0.20, 0.45, 0.78, and under the guess the sum is written: '0.20×(−0.62) + 0.45×0.66 + 0.78×(−0.82)', '+ bias (−0.53) = −1.00 → 0.27', 'node value × line weight, added up, then squashed into 0 to 1'.) White pulses leave the lit inputs and run down every line to the hidden nodes, then on to the output; the output ring flares and a number writes on beside it: '0.27'.
shots.motion: Pulses race down at a steady speed, brighter on the thicker lines; the hidden nodes flare as they arrive; the output flares last and the number appears at its value.
shots.transition: Continuous: the meter draws under the output.
shots.sound: A quick rising arpeggio as the pulses travel, a click as the number lands.
shots.check: The number is 0.27, the network's real output for the cat.

frames.note: Pulses leave the lit inputs.
They reach the hidden row and go on.
The output flares: '0.27'.

shots.caption: It guesses 0.27. The *answer* is 1.
shots.teaches: Compare the guess with the right answer: 0.27, when it should be 1.
shots.screen: A horizontal outline meter under the output (x 200 to 794 at y 1200, '0' and '1' at its ends): a cyan tick at 0.27 labelled 'guess 0.27', a white tick at 1 labelled 'answer: 1'.
shots.motion: The meter draws on left to right; the cyan tick drops from the output to its place; the white tick lights at 1.
shots.carries: The meter with the two ticks.
shots.transition: Continuous: the gap between them fills.
shots.sound: A tick for each mark.
shots.check: The cyan tick sits at 0.27 of the meter's length (x 360).

frames.note: The meter draws on under the output.
The guess and the answer on it.

shots.caption: The gap is the *error*.
shots.teaches: The gap between the guess and the answer is the error.
shots.screen: The gap on the meter, from 0.27 to 1, fills with a thick magenta line; under it 'error 0.73' in magenta.
shots.motion: The magenta gap fills from the cyan tick to the white one in one quick stroke and buzzes once.
shots.transition: Continuous: the error flows back up into the network.
shots.sound: A low buzz: the wrong note.
shots.check: The magenta segment runs exactly from 0.27 to 1; the label says 0.73.

frames.note: The gap starts to fill from the guess.
The error, 0.73, in magenta.

shots.caption: Now the error goes *backwards*.
shots.teaches: The key step: the error is sent backwards through the network.
shots.screen: Magenta pulses leave the output and run up every line, to the hidden nodes and on to the inputs: the same lines the guess came down, the other way. The meter keeps its magenta gap.
shots.motion: The magenta pulses rise row by row at a steady pace; each line they pass glows magenta for a moment, then settles back to cyan.
shots.carries: The network, every line just touched by the error.
shots.transition: Continuous: the lines start to change width.
shots.sound: A reversed zap, rising.
shots.check: The pulses go up (output to inputs), magenta, never cyan.

frames.note: Magenta pulses leave the output, going up.
They reach the inputs: every line has had its share.

shots.caption: Each weight gets nudged a *little*, to shrink the error.
shots.teaches: Each weight is nudged a little, in the direction that makes the error smaller.
shots.screen: (As built: the arrows carry the words 'thicker' and 'thinner'; then the camera goes close on the middle hidden → output line, '0.66 → 0.79' beside it, 'its weight' and a 0-to-1 gauge whose bar grows from 0.66 to 0.79 over a ghost of the old value, 'one nudge, made big so you can see it'.) The toy network: every line the error touched changes width a little (the ones from the lit inputs); small magenta arrows beside them show up or down; the line from the middle hidden node to the output is labelled with its weight changing: '0.66 → 0.79'.
shots.motion: All the touched lines swell or thin at once, eased over 0.6 s; the label's number ticks from 0.66 to 0.79 once (no counting through other values); the arrows flash once.
shots.transition: Continuous: a new guess runs down.
shots.sound: A soft rising synth swell, a click on the new number.
shots.check: The widths change by the computed amounts; the label reads 0.66 → 0.79.

frames.note: Before the nudge: the weight reads its old value.
The touched lines swell or thin; arrows show which way.
The labelled weight now 0.79.

shots.caption: Guess again: 0.40. *Closer*.
shots.teaches: The same cat again: the guess is now 0.40, closer to 1: the error shrank.
shots.screen: Pulses run down the nudged network again; on the meter the old guess stays as a faint cyan ghost at 0.27, the new cyan tick lands at 0.40, and the magenta gap is shorter: 'error 0.60'.
shots.motion: One fast run of pulses down; the cyan tick slides from the ghost to its new place; the magenta gap shortens with it.
shots.carries: The meter, the error a bit shorter.
shots.transition: The examples start to cycle at the top.
shots.sound: The arpeggio again, one step higher; a softer buzz.
shots.check: Ghost at 0.27, new tick at 0.40, gap 0.60.

frames.note: Pulses run down the nudged network.
The new guess, 0.40, beside the ghost of the old one; a shorter error.

shots.caption: The *error* keeps falling.

shots.caption: *1,000 rounds* later: cat 0.98, dog 0.01.
